title: Replicas, Partitions, and Shards

sections.title: Read Replicas and the Write-Ahead Log

html:
Replicas, Partitions, and Shards

A customer updates a shipping address, receives a confirmation, and opens the account page. The page still shows the previous address. After another refresh, the new address appears.

The write committed on the primary, but the first read was routed to a replica that had not yet applied the change. The primary accepted the update. The replica answered the read with older data. From the customer’s perspective, saving the address seemed not to work. The application needed a routing rule for the first read after a successful update.

Read replicas can increase available read capacity, but replication lag means that the application must classify which reads may use them. An account page immediately after an address update has a different freshness requirement from a product-category page. This chapter examines those requirements alongside the capacity and ownership changes introduced by replicas, partitioning, and sharding.

Baodium reached this decision after caching had reduced repeated catalog reads. Browsing traffic continued increasing, and a similar cache-miss percentage was being applied to a much larger request population. The database still received substantial work from distinct products, filters, and other queries that had no reusable cached result.

The database review compared read replicas, table partitioning, and sharding against the actual queries and transactions. Replicas could serve eligible reads, partitioning could reduce maintenance work on older records, and sharding could divide write responsibility. The associated consistency and ownership rules differed substantially.

Finding the Binding Constraint

Stored data volume and query workload can require different changes. Figure \(\ref{fig:ch07-sources}\) shows how many sources share one pool.

A large historical table may make archival and index maintenance expensive while receiving few customer queries. A much smaller table may serve thousands of requests per second and compete heavily for database resources. Increasing storage capacity will not resolve connection or lock contention. The investigation must identify whether the constraint comes from data volume, query execution, connection demand, or transactions awaiting other work.

At Baodium, individual catalog queries were still inexpensive, but connection-acquisition delay increased as more requests competed for access to the primary. That pointed to a concurrency problem, though not to its cause.

The engineers also examined connection occupancy, transaction duration, other callers, and database CPU and I/O. A pool can fill because callers submit more work, retain connections after queries finish, or wait inside transactions. Adding replicas would not correct every one of those conditions.

The investigation confirmed that eligible catalog reads were consuming a substantial share of primary access. Writes and other primary-required work used the same database, so redirecting those reads could preserve capacity for operations that needed it.

The relevant choices were as follows.

The techniques change different parts of the data path.
Technique What changes Application responsibility
Read replicas Additional copies serve eligible reads. Freshness, routing, and fallback.
Table partitioning Rows are organized into separate tables under one logical table. Partition-aware queries, keys, and maintenance.
Sharding Separate databases own subsets of records. Ownership routing, cross-shard work, and migration.

These techniques can be combined. A shard can contain partitioned tables and have its own replicas. There is no requirement to adopt them in a fixed sequence.

For the catalog read workload, replicas addressed the immediate problem without dividing write ownership. Partitioning and sharding required separate justification.

Read Replicas and the Write-Ahead Log

A read replica maintains a database copy and serves queries against it. In the PostgreSQL configuration we will use here, one primary accepts application writes and physical streaming replication updates the replicas. Figure \(\ref{fig:ch07-replicas}\) shows the arrangement.

PostgreSQL writes change records to its write-ahead log, or WAL, before the corresponding changed data pages can be written to durable storage. After a crash, recovery replays the required log records. A physical standby receives this log over the network and replays it against its own data. Receiving a record and applying it are separate steps, which matters when a reader needs the newly committed value.

There are several stages between a primary write and a replica query observing it.

Generation.

The primary produces WAL records for the changes.

Receipt and persistence.

The standby receives WAL and writes it according to its durability and acknowledgment settings.

Replay.

The standby applies the changes so subsequent query snapshots can observe them.

Receiving WAL is therefore not sufficient evidence that a query can read the corresponding data. For read routing, replay progress matters.

With asynchronous replication, the primary can acknowledge a committed write before a replica has received or replayed it, and that interval explains the address example at the beginning of the chapter.

Replicas also perform work beyond customer queries. They must receive and replay changes, maintain their database state, and read data into memory. Heavy queries can compete with that work, so another replica does not automatically provide the same capacity as an idle copy.

What Each Read Requires

We need to decide what each read must observe before choosing its database connection. Figure \(\ref{fig:ch07-lag}\) shows the window in which a replica read can be stale.

Baodium classified reads according to the operation they supported.

Read routing follows the result the caller requires.
Read requirement Example Routing approach
Accepted replica delay Browsing a product description. Use an eligible replica under the route’s policy.
Read-your-writes Viewing a newly saved address. Return committed state, use the primary, or verify replica replay progress.
Authoritative transaction Reserving available inventory. Execute through the owning service and database transaction.

This classification belongs near the query or service operation. A global rule that sends every SELECT to a replica cannot distinguish a browsing page from a check inside a purchase transaction.

A transaction that reads and then updates related state must use the appropriate database transaction throughout. Splitting its reads onto replicas can invalidate the assumptions used by the write.

Authoritative Reads and Transactions

Routing to the primary avoids replica delay, but does not by itself prevent concurrent updates. Suppose two customers attempt to reserve the final unit of a product. Both can read an available count of one before either submits a reservation. The application needs an atomic reservation operation, rather than a current read followed by an unprotected write.

[
  language=SQL,
  caption={Conditionally reserving one unit on the owning database.}]
UPDATE inventory
SET available = available - 1
WHERE product_id = :product_id
  AND available > 0
RETURNING product_id;

A returned row confirms that this statement decremented an available unit. No returned row means it made no reservation, which may indicate absence or insufficient availability according to the surrounding operation. A production reservation also records its operation identity and reservation details in the same transaction, and those records prevent a repeated request from decrementing stock again.

Primary routing and transaction correctness therefore answer related questions; the first selects the authoritative database, and the second defines how concurrent operations may change its records.

Payment and inventory access also continues through the services that own those operations. Adding a replica does not justify another service bypassing those ownership rules.

Read-Your-Writes

For the customer who just changed an address, the first option is to return the committed address from the write operation. The page can display that result without issuing another database query. Returning the committed value avoids the additional read and the replica-lag problem for that immediate response. Later requests still require a freshness-aware routing rule.

A later request may reach another application instance or another device. Its correctness cannot depend on the original handler still running. Routing that read to the primary can satisfy the requirement under an appropriate transaction snapshot. Routing to the primary for a fixed period after a write reduces stale reads, but the timer alone is not a guarantee. Replica delay can outlast the chosen interval.

A more explicit approach returns a replication position associated with the committed write. The router uses a replica only after that replica has replayed through the required position. Otherwise, it waits under a deadline, uses permitted primary access, or returns an unavailable result.

The position must cover the commit, and the query must obtain its snapshot after the replay condition is satisfied. An earlier transaction snapshot could still return the previous state. Such tokens also need to be tied to the correct database history. After failover, the application cannot compare positions from unrelated histories without validating their relationship.

This additional machinery is useful when primary routing for these reads becomes expensive. For a modest number of account updates, returning committed state and using the primary for subsequent sensitive reads may be easier to operate.

::: decision

**Which reads may move to a replica?**

Browsing traffic is saturating the primary. Two replicas are available, and replication lag is typically under a second. Four read paths are candidates for the move: the product detail page, the “items in your cart” panel, the inventory check that decides whether Add to Cart is enabled, and the order confirmation page shown immediately after a purchase.

**Move all four. The lag is under a second, and no customer notices a second.**

**Move the product page and the cart panel. Keep the inventory check and the confirmation page on the primary.**

**Move only the product page, because it receives the most requests.**

—

Sort them by what a stale answer costs rather than by traffic volume.

The confirmation page is the clearest case against A. It is read immediately after the customer’s own write, which is precisely the window in which a replica has not applied it. The customer completes a purchase and is shown an order that does not exist. Read-your-writes is a requirement here, not a preference.

The inventory check has a more serious consequence. An outdated count can affect whether the application accepts a reservation. That makes it an authoritative read, and Section \(\ref{sec:ch07-authoritative}\) explains why routing it to the primary still does not protect against two customers reserving the last unit at once.

Under the stated policy, the product page tolerates a second of staleness. The cart panel can use a replica for ordinary reads, but a read immediately after a quantity change must satisfy the customer’s read-after-write requirement.

So B, with the cart panel routed to the primary for a short interval after a write. C leaves capacity on the table for no gain.

:::

Replica Eligibility and Fallback

Baodium introduced two replicas for browsing queries whose freshness policy permitted them. The router selected among replicas that were reachable, had current monitoring information, and met the route’s eligibility criteria. Checking monitoring freshness is essential, because a replica last reported little delay several minutes ago may since have disconnected. The old sample must not continue making it eligible.

A routing observation therefore includes when the sample was collected, the measured replay progress, and connection health. A background observer collects these values so customer requests do not each issue a monitoring query.

Interpreting Lag Measurements

Replication positions describe progress through the WAL. A byte distance indicates unapplied log work, but does not directly express seconds or a number of missing transactions. A heartbeat can provide a time-based estimate. The primary periodically updates a row, and an observer reads it from each replica. The estimate depends on heartbeat frequency, sampling delay, and clock handling.

Be careful which number reaches the dashboard. “Forty megabytes behind” and “two seconds behind” are not interchangeable, and an idle replica can appear to be behind in time while having nothing left to apply. Neither a previous lag sample nor a low average establishes that one specific write is available. A strict read-your-writes requirement needs evidence tied to that write or an authoritative route. This distinction prevents monitoring from being used as a stronger consistency guarantee than it provides.

Bounded Primary Fallback

Suppose replicas normally serve 80 percent of a browsing workload and the primary serves the other 20 percent. If every replica read falls back to the primary, that class of primary traffic becomes five times its previous rate. During fallback, requests keep succeeding while their reads move to the primary, which still has to process writes, reconciliation, and other required reads. Unrestricted fallback can turn replica unavailability into a primary outage, so Baodium treated fallback as an admitted workload. When its allocation was exhausted, the route returned its approved reduced or unavailable result.

The routing procedure can be expressed without embedding every database detail in the handler.

[
  language=Python,
  caption={Replica eligibility with explicit primary fallback.
           APIs are illustrative.}]
def choose_read_target(policy, observations, request):
    candidates = [
        replica
        for replica in observations.replicas
        if replica.available
        and replica.sample_is_current()
        and policy.accepts(replica)
    ]

    if candidates:
        return replica_admission.try_choose(
            candidates,
            deadline=request.deadline,
        )

    if policy.allow_primary_fallback:
        return primary_fallback.try_admit(
            deadline=request.deadline,
        )

    raise ReadTemporarilyUnavailable()

The admission methods either return an admitted target or an explicit rejection, so they do not hide another unbounded queue, and their permits cover the actual query through local completion and cleanup.

A route requiring the primary uses its own admission path. A route requiring a write position additionally verifies that position before executing on a replica. The simplified example covers browsing reads governed by operational replica eligibility.

An accepted older result must be part of the route’s policy; the router cannot relax the required freshness because all preferred targets are unavailable.

Replication, Failover, and Recovery

Read scaling and failover use related infrastructure, but have different requirements; with asynchronous replication, a promoted standby may lack writes that the primary acknowledged. The relevant question is which acknowledged commit records are available and durable on the candidate. Replay delay alone does not determine potential data loss. WAL already received and durably stored may still be waiting for replay and can be applied before the new primary serves requests.

Synchronous replication can require standby acknowledgment before a write returns. The selected mode determines whether that acknowledgment covers receipt, durable storage, or application of the commit. In PostgreSQL, a configuration that waits for remote application can make the write available to subsequent snapshots on the participating standby. Waiting only for durable WAL storage does not provide the same immediate read guarantee, and an unrelated asynchronous replica may still lag. The cost is additional commit waiting and a policy decision when the required standbys are unavailable. Reducing the acknowledgment requirement during an outage changes the durability contract.

Failover also has to stop the previous primary from accepting writes once a replacement is promoted. The usual word for this is fencing: building a barrier around the old writer so that it cannot accept writes, even if it restarts still configured as the primary. Routing changes alone are insufficient if old connections can still reach it. The deployment needs a way to fence the former writer and validate the new authority.

Replication does not replace backup, because a mistaken delete can be replayed on every replica. Recovery to an earlier point requires backups and the appropriate retained change history, verified through restore tests.

::: fieldnote

**GitHub, October 2018**

A 43-second network interruption separated GitHub’s East Coast network hub from its primary data center. Orchestrator promoted West Coast databases. The former primaries contained writes that had not replicated west, while the new primaries subsequently accepted writes of their own. Returning to the former primaries therefore required reconciling two divergent histories.

GitHub prioritized data integrity during recovery and paused work including webhook delivery and Pages builds. Its report describes 24 hours and 11 minutes of degraded service and states that no user data was lost, with manual reconciliation still in progress when the report was published. Promotion selected a writer before engineers had resolved the complete write history. A failover test must examine acknowledged writes and fencing of the former writer as well as the promotion procedure.

Source: published incident report.

:::

Table Partitioning

Read replicas addressed Baodium’s eligible read volume, but the orders table presented a different problem. It contained six years of customer orders, and the monthly archival job deleted rows older than 24 months one batch at a time. Each run took most of a night, generated a large volume of WAL that the replicas then had to replay, and left index bloat behind it.

Partitioning divides one logical table into separate physical tables by a partition key. For a query containing the relevant key bounds, PostgreSQL can exclude unrelated partitions, which is called partition pruning. The useful key is the one that matches the work we are trying to eliminate, so the team started with the operations rather than the table.

[
  language=SQL,
  caption={Three operations the partition key had to serve.}]
-- Archival: remove orders older than the retention period
DELETE FROM orders
 WHERE created_at < '2024-07-01 00:00:00+00';

-- Monthly finance report
SELECT state, count(*), sum(amount_minor)
  FROM orders
 WHERE created_at >= '2026-06-01 00:00:00+00'
   AND created_at <  '2026-07-01 00:00:00+00'
 GROUP BY state;

-- Order lookup from a receipt or support ticket
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE order_id = $1;

Table \(\ref{tab:partition-keys}\) evaluates three candidate keys against those operations.

created_at removes the archival work and narrows the report. It does nothing for the point lookup, and that gap shapes the rest of the design.

[
  language=SQL,
  caption={Monthly order partitions with explicit time boundaries.}]
CREATE TABLE orders (
    order_id     UUID        NOT NULL,
    user_id      UUID        NOT NULL,
    created_at   TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    state        TEXT        NOT NULL,
    amount_minor BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (order_id, created_at)
) PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at);

CREATE TABLE orders_2026_01
    PARTITION OF orders
    FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-01-01 00:00:00+00')
                 TO ('2026-02-01 00:00:00+00');

The upper boundary is exclusive, so the next partition begins at that timestamp. Explicit timezone boundaries avoid depending on a session’s interpretation of an unqualified timestamp.

For the lookup, the application can include the creation period in the order reference it gives customers, maintain an order-to-partition directory, or accept multi-partition probes for infrequent operations. With 72 monthly partitions and support lookups at a few requests per second, Baodium measured the probe cost before deciding whether a directory was worth its write overhead.

Identity and Constraints

The primary key in the example includes the partition key because PostgreSQL’s uniqueness rules for partitioned tables require it. That changes the constraint; the database enforces uniqueness of the pair (order_id, created_at), but it does not enforce uniqueness of order_id across all dates.

If the application requires database-enforced global order identity, it needs another mechanism. One option is a nonpartitioned order directory with a unique order ID, written in the same transaction as order creation. The same directory records the creation period, which also closes the point-lookup gap from Table \(\ref{tab:partition-keys}\).

The directory adds one indexed insert per order and its own storage. At Baodium’s order rate that cost was small, but it had to be counted, and the transaction rule tying the two records together had to be tested.

Partition Operations

Partitions must exist before rows arrive for their ranges; without a matching partition or an intentional default partition, an insert fails. Baodium created partitions three months ahead and alerted when fewer than two future partitions remained.

Archival became a metadata operation. Detaching an expired partition replaced the nightly batch deletes, removed most of their WAL, and left no bloat in the remaining indexes. The operation still needs coordination for locks, backups, references, and the retention policy.

Partitioning reduced maintenance work and, where pruning applied, query work, but it did not add another database server or distribute writes across machines. The release test therefore checked query plans for the three operations above, the first insert into a new range, and a partition detach under production-like load.

Sharding and Data Ownership

The sharding discussion began with a question in a design review: given merchant order MO-48192, which database owns its next write?

Each confirmed checkout produced one merchant order for each merchant in the cart, published through the outbox from Chapter 3. Merchants accepted, shipped, refunded, and settled those orders through the merchant portal. Every step wrote to the merchant order, its line items, its fulfillment state, and the merchant’s payout ledger, all on one primary.

Two measurements forced the question. Merchant-order writes peaked at about 3,000 per second, against roughly 4,000 that the primary had sustained in workload tests after index and batching improvements. And when the largest merchants ran end-of-day settlement or bulk refunds, their transactions held locks and consumed I/O that every other merchant shared. Replicas could not help with either, because both were write problems.

Sharding assigns subsets of records to separate databases, each with its own write path. The application then has to answer the review’s question for every write, in every process, consistently across deployments, and it has to be able to change the answer without rewriting every stored reference.

Because sharding is close to irreversible, Baodium considered it only after caching, replicas, and partitioning had been applied where they fit.

Choosing the Shard Key

The shard key decides which transactions stay inside one database. The team listed the merchant-order operations by frequency and correctness requirement, then tested three candidate keys against them.

merchant_order_id distributes writes perfectly and turns settlement into a distributed transaction across every shard. Settlement moves money, so that was the operation the team was least willing to make cross-shard.

merchant_id keeps every merchant-scoped operation local, including settlement. Its cost is that a merchant’s whole workload lands on one shard, so one very large merchant can dominate it.

(merchant_id, sub-bucket) hashes each merchant across 16 sub-buckets. It spreads a large merchant’s writes, and it makes settlement and the portal list cross up to 16 buckets.

Baodium chose merchant_id. The most important write transaction was merchant-scoped, and the team accepted the large-merchant hotspot as a known risk to measure rather than a reason to give up local settlement. Section \(\ref{sec:ch07-uneven}\) follows that risk.

Two consequences followed from the choice. Operations spanning merchants, such as an operator’s view of all recent orders, now needed several shards. And uniqueness changed; a merchant-scoped order number remained enforceable by one shard, while a carrier tracking number that must be unique across all merchants could not be enforced by any single shard. That invariant needed a separate directory with its own unique index.

A transaction that genuinely spans shards requires a defined coordination procedure: a distributed transaction or durable steps with recovery and compensation, as Chapter 3 described for external effects.

Routing and Shard Assignment

The router must produce the same assignment across processes and deployments. A language hash function whose seed changes between process starts is unsuitable for persistent placement. Figure \(\ref{fig:ch07-buckets}\) shows the route from key to database.

A fixed modulo calculation over the physical shard count is easy to implement, but changing the count reassigns most keys, and each reassignment requires data transfer before the new rule can be used.

A fixed set of virtual buckets separates record assignment from physical placement.

[
  language=Python,
  caption={Stable bucket assignment with a versioned ownership directory.}]
import hashlib

BUCKET_COUNT = 1024

def bucket_for(merchant_id):
    canonical_id = canonicalize_merchant_id(merchant_id)
    digest = hashlib.sha256(
        canonical_id.encode("utf-8")
    ).digest()
    return int.from_bytes(digest[:8], "big") % BUCKET_COUNT

def locate_merchant(merchant_id, directory):
    override = directory.merchant_override(merchant_id)
    if override is not None:
        return override              # (database, epoch)
    bucket = bucket_for(merchant_id)
    return directory.owner_with_epoch(bucket)

The bucket count and ID canonicalization are part of the persisted routing contract. Changing either requires a migration. The merchant override is explained in Section \(\ref{sec:ch07-uneven}\).

The directory maps each bucket to a database and an ownership version, or epoch. Moving a bucket changes one directory entry rather than every record’s assignment. The directory is also a dependency. Routers cache it with a version, and each database stores the epoch it currently owns for each bucket so that it can reject writes routed under an obsolete entry.

Uneven Load Across Shards

Equal row counts do not imply equal database demand; the merchant_id key made this concrete within weeks.

Baodium started with eight shards, and the largest merchant produced about 18 percent of merchant-order writes. At the 3,000-per-second peak, that merchant alone generated 540 writes per second. The remaining 2,460 spread across eight shards at roughly 308 each, so the shard holding the large merchant carried about 848 writes per second against an average of 375.

Each shard had sustained about 900 writes per second in its workload test. Nominal fleet capacity was therefore 7,200, but the hot shard reached its tested limit when total traffic rose by only about six percent. The busiest shard sets the limit for the fleet.

The team measured query rate, transaction cost, connection occupancy, and storage by shard, then evaluated three responses:

  • Move the other buckets off the hot shard. That removes at most 308 writes per second and leaves the large merchant as the shard’s dominant load.

  • Give the merchant a dedicated shard through a merchant-level directory override, checked before the bucket entry. Its 540 writes per second fit within one database’s tested 900, and settlement stays local.

  • Split the merchant across sub-buckets, as in the third candidate key. That would turn its settlement into a cross-bucket operation.

Baodium chose the dedicated shard. If a single merchant ever approached one database’s tested write limit, the split key and a redesigned settlement procedure would become necessary, and the team recorded that threshold as a review trigger.

Cross-Shard Queries

A query containing the shard key targets one database. Without the key, the request may need to visit every shard. Sending that query concurrently to each shard and combining the results is called scatter-gather.

An operator page requests the latest 100 merchant orders across all merchants. Fetching every recent row from every shard and sorting in application memory is unnecessary. Each shard returns its own latest 100 under a common ordering, and the application merges the candidates.

The ordering needs a tie-breaker, such as creation time followed by order ID. Pagination needs cursor state that avoids rescanning the same rows. Separate shard queries do not share a global snapshot, so the page contract has to state how concurrent writes may appear.

Fan-out needs limits across requests. Creating eight worker threads for each page request can produce hundreds of active queries under load. A shared bounded executor, a bounded queue, per-shard admission, and one request deadline control the combined work.

Canceling a waiting future does not necessarily cancel a running database query. The driver timeout and query cancellation procedure must account for work that continues after the aggregator stops waiting. The result also needs a completeness rule; an exploratory dashboard may show partial results with missing shards identified. A reconciliation total cannot be reported as complete when one shard failed to answer.

When to Stop Fanning Out

The operator page ran a few times a minute, and eight shard queries per request was acceptable. Carrier tracking updates were different. Each update arrived keyed only by tracking number, which does not contain the merchant.

At the 300-per-second peak of tracking updates, scatter-gather would send 2,400 shard queries per second before retries, and seven of every eight would find nothing. Adding shards would raise that number further. A tracking-number directory, written when an order ships, costs one indexed insert per shipment and turns each update into one directory lookup and one shard write. Baodium shipped roughly 40 orders per second at peak, so the directory replaced 2,400 fan-out reads per second with about 340 directory operations, and it also enforced the global uniqueness of tracking numbers.

In general, fan-out cost grows with request rate multiplied by shard count. A maintained read model or directory costs its update rate plus its own storage and update delay. When the first number exceeds the second on a path whose freshness requirement the read model can meet, the read model is the cheaper design.

Resharding and Ownership Transfer

Moving the large merchant to its dedicated shard was Baodium’s first ownership transfer under live writes. The new directory entry could not be published until the destination had a complete, verified copy of the merchant’s data and had been assigned write authority.

The procedure ran in five stages:

  1. Copy. Copy the merchant’s rows while the source shard continues serving, and record the source change position at which the copy began.

  2. Catch up. Capture changes made after that position and apply them to the destination until the remaining gap is small.

  3. Fence. Mark the merchant as moving on the source, which rejects new writes for it, and let in-flight transactions finish.

  4. Final apply and verify. Record the final source change position, apply through it, and compare row counts and per-order checksums.

  5. Transfer authority. Increment the ownership epoch, publish the directory entry, and allow the destination to accept writes.

The arithmetic set the schedule. The merchant had about 140 million rows across orders, line items, and ledger entries. At a measured copy rate of 25,000 rows per second, the copy took about 93 minutes. The team ran it off-peak, when the merchant averaged 300 writes per second, which left about 1.7 million changes to apply. The applier sustained 3,000 changes per second while new changes continued arriving at 300, so the gap closed at a net 2,700 per second, in roughly ten and a half minutes. The fence in stage 3 then paused the merchant’s writes for a few seconds rather than for the length of the copy.

The former owner enforces its loss of authority locally. Publishing a new directory entry is insufficient while some routers hold cached routes or open connections.

[
  language=Python,
  caption={A shard checks ownership in the same transaction as the write.
           Repository methods are illustrative.}]
def write_merchant_order(db, route, change):
    with db.transaction():
        # Shared lock: a transfer waits for this write,
        # and this write sees any completed transfer.
        owner = db.lock_ownership_shared(route.placement_key)
        if owner.status != "owned" or owner.epoch != route.epoch:
            raise StaleRoute(route.placement_key, owner.epoch)
        db.apply(change)

A router that receives StaleRoute refreshes its directory entry and retries under the operation’s original identity, so the retry cannot apply the change twice.

Rollback becomes more involved after the destination accepts writes. Pointing routes back to the source would omit those writes unless they were synchronized back under another controlled transfer. Migration tests therefore included process failure during the copy, delayed router cache refresh, duplicate requests across the fence, and interruption between stages 4 and 5. At each stage the test asserted a single known owner, not merely matching row counts.

Validation and Operating Evidence

Each topology change needs a test that targets the new failure path. For replicas, Baodium paused replay after committing a customer update and verified read-your-writes behavior, and it also tested expired monitoring samples and loss of every eligible replica. Primary fallback had to respect its allocation while required writes continued.

Replica query tests included replay contention and cancellations caused by recovery conflicts. Depending on the database settings, accommodating queries can affect replay or primary cleanup, so reporting queries need particular attention.

For partitioning, the team inspected query plans for archival, the monthly report, and point lookup, and tested the first insert into a new time range. Uniqueness requirements were checked separately from date-range performance.

For sharding, the test dataset reproduced the real merchant-size distribution, including the 18-percent merchant. The tests covered an unavailable shard, incomplete fan-out results, stale routes after a transfer, and tracking-directory lookups for orders that had not yet shipped. A balanced synthetic dataset would have hidden the hot shard.

Production measurements followed the same boundaries; replica health included replay progress and sample age. Routing metrics showed which read classes reached each target and how much primary fallback was being used.

Partition measurements included query plans, storage, and detach duration. Shard measurements included write rate against each shard’s tested limit, connection occupancy, errors, and the share of traffic from the largest merchant on each shard. A fleet-wide average would have reported 375 writes per second while one shard carried 848.

Recovery evidence completed the picture. The team recorded failover write exposure, restore-test results, and migration ownership epochs so an incident could be explained in terms of actual data placement and accepted writes.

Summary

The stale address on Baodium’s account page illustrated the requirement that read routing must follow the kind of result a request needs. A replica could serve browsing traffic while an account page immediately after a successful update required read-your-writes behavior. Adding a replica therefore increased capacity for some reads and created a routing and recovery obligation for the application.

Partitioning addressed a different problem. By partitioning records on creation time, Baodium made retention and monthly reports more manageable, but point lookups and global uniqueness still required separate design work. Sharding introduced a further boundary: merchant orders could be processed on assigned databases, provided that every write had a current owner, the routing directory was authoritative, and the team had procedures for hot shards and ownership transfer.

The choice among replicas, partitions, and shards follows the measured constraint. For any proposal, trace one important read and one important write through the new layout, then repeat with a delayed replica, an unavailable shard, and stale routing information. The resulting failure paths establish what the application needs to record and what engineers need to observe. Chapter 8 follows those operations across service and data boundaries to determine which parts of a customer request have actually completed.

::: hiddenassumptions

Assumption and scope & Eligible browsing reads can use replicas under an explicit freshness policy, while authoritative transactions and read-your-writes requests receive the evidence they require.
Condition that tests it & Replication is delayed, a primary fails, or ownership transfers between shards.
